## Purpose

This report compares `scripts/final_data.R` and
`scripts/final_data_codex.R`. Both scripts build a country-year analysis
dataset for 2000--2019 by combining mortality outcomes, natural-disaster
indicators, a lagged conflict indicator, and country-level covariates. The
comparison focuses on each stage of the workflow, the code choices made, and
the consequences of those choices for the final data.

The scripts share the same overall goal, but `final_data_codex.R` makes the
country-year structure explicit before creating the disaster and conflict
variables. This matters because the final dataset needs one observation per
country and year.

## Workflow overview

| Section | `final_data.R` | `final_data_codex.R` |
|---|---|---|
| Packages and input | Loads four packages and reads CSV files with `read.csv()` | Loads `tidyverse` and `here`, then reads the same CSV files |
| Mortality data | Reshapes four wide mortality files with `make_long()` | Reshapes the same files with a more flexible `make_long()` |
| Disasters | Makes row-level drought and earthquake flags | Aggregates to one country-year and fills absent events with zero |
| Conflict | Sums `best` and uses `lag()` over observed conflict years | Shifts the previous year's total onto a complete country-year panel |
| Covariates and merge | Imports covariates and full-joins all tables | Imports covariates and full-joins all tables, then sorts rows |
| Export | Writes `merged_conflict_data.csv` | Writes `final_data_codex.csv` |

## Packages and data import

Both scripts use `tidyverse` for data manipulation and `here` for
project-relative paths. Using `here("data", "raw", ...)` is a good practice
because it avoids relying on a manually set working directory. Both scripts
also use base R's `read.csv()`, so this is not a difference in the import
method.

`final_data.R` loads `countrycode` and `janitor`. `countrycode` is not used in
the script. It uses `clean_names()` after loading `janitor`. In contrast,
`final_data_codex.R` calls `janitor::clean_names()` directly, so it does not
need to attach the entire `janitor` package. The latter makes it clear where
the function comes from and avoids an unnecessary attached package.

`final_data.R` also runs `summary()` on each raw mortality table. These calls
are useful for interactive inspection, but they do not alter the data or
contribute to the final merged object. `final_data_codex.R` omits them for a
more streamlined processing script.

## Mortality data: wide to long

Both scripts import four mortality datasets—maternal, infant, neonatal, and
under-five mortality—and use one function repeatedly to reshape them from wide
to long format. In each case, the final data have `iso`, `year`, and one
outcome column.

In `final_data.R`, the function explicitly selects `X2000:X2019` and then
removes the `X` from the names. This is clear when the study period is fixed:

```r
make_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    select(iso, X2000:X2019) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("X"),
      names_to = "year",
      names_prefix = "X",
      values_to = value_name
    ) |>
    mutate(year = as.numeric(year))
}
```

In `final_data_codex.R`, the function identifies any column whose name is an
`X` followed by a four-digit year:

```r
make_long <- function(data, value_name) {
  data |>
    select(iso, matches("^X[0-9]{4}$")) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = matches("^X[0-9]{4}$"),
      names_to = "year",
      names_prefix = "X",
      names_transform = list(year = as.integer),
      values_to = value_name
    )
}
```

The Codex version is more robust if future data include additional annual
columns because it does not hard-code 2000--2019. It also converts `year` to
an integer inside `pivot_longer()`, rather than converting it in a later
`mutate()` step. For the current files, both approaches produce the same
mortality values and year range.

## Disaster data

Both scripts read `disaster.csv`, standardize the names with `clean_names()`,
and retain only droughts and earthquakes from 2000--2019. They then create
binary variables named `drought` and `earthquake`.

The important difference is the level of observation. In `final_data.R`, each
disaster record remains a row. A country with multiple qualifying disasters in
one year can therefore have multiple rows after the merge. In addition, a
country-year with no qualifying disaster has no disaster row and will receive
missing values after a full join rather than explicit zeros.

`final_data_codex.R` first turns each record into two indicators and then
collapses all records for a country-year using `max()`. Because the indicators
are zero or one, `max()` means “did this event occur at least once?” The code
then joins those indicators to the mortality country-year panel and uses
`coalesce()` to convert missing event indicators to zero:

```r
disaster_events |>
  group_by(iso, year) |>
  summarise(
    drought = max(drought),
    earthquake = max(earthquake),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

disaster <- matmor |>
  distinct(iso, year) |>
  left_join(disaster_events, by = c("iso", "year")) |>
  mutate(
    drought = coalesce(drought, 0L),
    earthquake = coalesce(earthquake, 0L)
  )
```

This approach is preferable for a country-year dataset: it guarantees at most
one disaster record per country-year and represents “no recorded drought or
earthquake” as `0`.

## Conflict data

The two scripts agree on the first step: several conflict rows can exist for a
country-year, so `best` is summed within `iso` and `year`. They also use the
same threshold: prior-year total conflict fatalities of at least 25 imply a
binary conflict indicator of 1.

In `final_data.R`, `lag(deaths_sum)` is calculated after sorting the years that
appear in the conflict table. This works when every intervening year has a
conflict row. However, if a country has records in 2000 and 2002 but none in
2001, the value for 2002 is lagged from 2000 rather than from 2001. The first
observed conflict year also receives `NA` because it has no lagged row.

`final_data_codex.R` avoids this by shifting each annual total forward one
year, then joining it to a complete mortality country-year panel. For example,
the total `best` value in 2000 is assigned to the `conflict_presence` value in
2001. Country-years without a prior-year total are assigned zero:

```r
conflict_totals |>
  transmute(
    iso,
    year = year + 1L,
    conflict_presence = as.integer(best_total >= 25)
  )
```

This directly expresses the research rule: the conflict value for year *t*
depends on `best` in year *t - 1*. It also preserves a valid value for 2000 by
using the available 1999 conflict records.

## Covariates and final merge

Both scripts import `covariates.csv`, which already contains `iso` and `year`,
and use `reduce(full_join, by = c("iso", "year"))` to combine the component
tables. A full join retains country-years that occur in any input source.

The original script stores the result as `conflict_merged` and converts `year`
to integer after joining. The Codex script stores the result as `merged_data`,
converts years during reshaping, and adds `arrange(iso, year)` after the merge.
Sorting does not change the values, but it makes the final file easier to
inspect and ensures a consistent row order.

The more consequential merge difference follows from the earlier preparation:
the original disaster table may contain repeated country-year keys, whereas
the Codex disaster and conflict tables are built against a country-year panel.
Consequently, the Codex merge better maintains the intended one-row-per-
country-year structure.

## Exported files

The scripts export different filenames in `data/processed/`:

| Script | Output file | Object written |
|---|---|---|
| `final_data.R` | `merged_conflict_data.csv` | `conflict_merged` |
| `final_data_codex.R` | `final_data_codex.csv` | `merged_data` |

Both use `row.names = FALSE`, which prevents R's row numbers from becoming an
unwanted CSV column.

## Conclusion

Both scripts correctly establish the intended workflow and use reusable code
for the mortality reshaping step. `final_data.R` is a clear, step-by-step
version that includes exploratory summaries. `final_data_codex.R` is more
defensive for panel-data analysis: it recognizes year columns programmatically,
aggregates multiple disasters within country-year, fills no-event years with
zero, and implements the prior-year conflict rule without skipping calendar
years. These differences make `final_data_codex.R` the stronger choice when
the final dataset is intended to contain one observation for every country and
year.
